passage: Vinita's fractions homework covered the whole dining table in their Hyderabad flat, and she had been staring at question six for ten minutes. She rubbed her eyes. Her brother Tejas was on the sofa. If she asked him, he might laugh. If she asked Mummy, she might say “Try harder.” She thought about her maths teacher, Mr. Rao, who never made anyone feel silly. She took a breath, walked over to Tejas and said, “I need help with this one. Can you show me the first step?” Tejas looked up, surprised, and came over. “Sure. Show me where you're stuck.” Vinita felt her shoulders drop.

qa.q: How long had Vinita been staring at question six?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Vinita hesitate before asking Tejas for help?
qa.a: She feared he might laugh, and that Mummy might just say to try harder, so she thought carefully about who would be safe to ask.

qa.q: What made Vinita's request easy to answer?
qa.a: She said plainly “I need help” and asked for only the first step, so she asked a specific person for a specific thing.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Vinita asked him?
qa.a: Tejas seemed surprised and then willing, so he was probably pleased to be trusted.

grounding: A child learns that saying I need help is a strength and picks whom to ask, in this case a brother.

passage: “Irfan, I can't do the cardboard bridge on my own,” Abhinav said, dragging the box across the floor. Irfan looked up from his book. “Did you ask Sir?” “No. He'll think I wasn't paying attention.” “He won't. He said on Monday to ask.” Abhinav bit his lip. “What if he laughs?” “He won't laugh. I'll come with you if you want.” They walked to the staff room together. Abhinav said, “Sir, I need help with the bridge, please.” Sir said, “Thank you for asking. Let's look.” Abhinav grinned at Irfan, who gave him a thumbs-up. 👍

qa.q: What were the boys making?
qa.a: A cardboard bridge.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav afraid to ask Sir?
qa.a: He worried that Sir would think he had not been paying attention, or might laugh at him.

qa.q: What helped Abhinav ask for help in the end?
qa.a: Irfan reminded him Sir had said to ask and offered to go with him.

qa.q: How might Sir feel when a pupil asks for help?
qa.a: Sir said thank you for asking, so he sees it as a good sign that the pupil wants to learn. 🙂

grounding: A child learns that saying I need help is a strength and picks a teacher to ask, with a friend's support.

passage: I'm Pema. For a whole term of swimming lessons, I pretended I could float. I'd hang on to the side and kick, and when the teacher looked, I'd bob my head under as if I'd just come up. I thought if I said I couldn't, everyone would laugh. In the holidays my cousin Hemant took me to the lake. I watched him float on his back like it was nothing, and my throat went tight. Then I said it: “I need help. I can't float.” He didn't laugh. He put one hand under my back and said, “Breathe in big. Now let go.” By the third day, I floated alone. I wish I'd asked in the first week.

qa.q: Where did Hemant take Pema?
qa.a: Hemant took Pema to the lake.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling during the term of pretending?
qa.a: Pema felt afraid of being laughed at and ashamed of not being able to float, so kept pretending.

qa.q: Why was saying “I need help” a strength for Pema?
qa.a: It got Pema real help from someone trusted, and within three days Pema could float alone.

qa.q: How did Hemant respond to Pema's request?
qa.a: Hemant didn't laugh; he supported Pema's back and gave simple instructions until Pema could float.

grounding: Shows a child who feared being judged finally saying I need help to a trusted person, and asking turning out to be a strength.

passage: Teacher's note, Monday. Nilesh, Class 4. Abhinav never asks for help. For two weeks he has handed in fraction sheets with the hard half blank, and when I ask, he says, “I forgot.” Today I watched him stare at question six for ten minutes, pencil still, cheeks red, glancing at the others. I think he's scared of looking slow in front of them. So I've put a small tin of green cards on each table. Put one on your desk if you're stuck, and I'll come over quietly. No hands up, no announcements. Within twenty minutes, Abhinav's green card was out. We worked through question six together, in whispers.

qa.q: What did Nilesh put on each table?
qa.a: Nilesh put a small tin of green cards on each table.

qa.q: What was Abhinav likely feeling as he stared at question six?
qa.a: Abhinav was likely stuck and scared of looking slow in front of the others, his cheeks going red.

qa.q: Why did the green cards help Abhinav ask for help?
qa.a: They made asking private, with no hands up or announcements, so he could ask without fearing judgement.

qa.q: What would change if Nilesh had asked Abhinav in front of the class why he was stuck?
qa.a: Abhinav would probably have felt more exposed and ashamed, and might have kept hiding that he needed help.

grounding: Shows a child who never asks for help because he fears judgement, and a teacher building a safe way to ask.

passage: Thursday. Aditi's diary. I lost my bus pass today. I searched my bag three times and felt sick. First I asked Yash, and he just said, “Uh-oh, you'll have to walk,” which didn't help at all. Then I thought, who would actually know what to do? Not Yash. Not the bus driver; he's always grumpy. The school office. I made myself walk in and say, “I need help. I've lost my bus pass.” The lady there didn't even look surprised. She phoned the transport teacher, who wrote me a slip for today and said a new pass would come on Monday. Asking the right person took five minutes. Worrying took all morning.

qa.q: When will the new bus pass come?
qa.a: The new pass will come on Monday.

qa.q: What was Aditi feeling after searching the bag three times?
qa.a: Aditi felt sick with worry about losing the bus pass.

qa.q: How did Aditi decide who to ask for help?
qa.a: Aditi thought about who would actually know what to do and chose the school office instead of Yash or the bus driver.

qa.q: Why was Yash's reply not much help?
qa.a: Yash only pointed out the problem, saying Aditi would have to walk, without knowing how to fix it.

grounding: Shows a child saying I need help and choosing the right person to ask.

passage:
For a whole week, Lavanya had copied the long-division answers from Ramu's slate in the little school behind the panchayat office. She didn't understand where the numbers went. Asking felt impossible; last year a boy had called her "duffer" when she asked a question, and the whole row had laughed.

On Friday, when the others ran out to the handpump, she stayed back. Not the loud Sir who taught science. Nandini Madam, who never laughed at anyone. Lavanya twisted her dupatta. "Madam… I need help. I don't get the dividing."

Nandini Madam put down her chalk. "Thank you for telling me. That takes courage. Come, sit. And I think half the class needs this too." On Monday she taught it again, slowly, for everyone.

qa.q: Whose slate had Lavanya been copying from?
qa.a: Ramu's slate.

qa.q: Why had Lavanya avoided asking for a week?
qa.a: She was afraid of being judged and laughed at, because last year a boy called her "duffer" when she asked and the whole row laughed.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do that was wise when she finally asked?
qa.a: She chose a safe person, Nandini Madam, who never laughed at anyone, and asked in private when the others had gone out.

qa.q: How did Nandini Madam see Lavanya's request?
qa.a: As courage, not weakness; she thanked her and guessed others needed help too, so she retaught it for everyone.

grounding: It shows a child who feared being judged finally saying she needs help to a trusted teacher, and the teacher treating it as a strength.
